description: I’m Ulaş, a computer engineer (MSc in EEE) with 20+ years in AI, machine learning and signal processing, mostly in aerospace and defense. I founded a deep-tech startup about aerospace. My interests: human factors in space, AI for crew health and wearable tech. I’ll work on an astronaut health and performance concept. I have a team, but happy to connect and share ideas with other participants. Visit https://paragonaerotech.com/
summary:
NeuroShield is an explainable health self-assessment tool for astronauts on station, lunar and Martian missions. It is a web app that runs offline in any browser.

It brings together wearable brain and body sensors (EEG, fNIRS, heart rate, SpO2, skin conductance), the vital signs the challenge names (blood pressure, heart rate, blood sugar, temperature, sleep, mood), cabin sensors and the crew's own photos (skin, eye, wound, ultrasound etc.). Every signal is colour-coded against limits from NASA and the medical literature, each with a linked source. Twenty-one explainable rules warn minutes before symptoms show, say what to do step by step, and say who leads: the flight surgeon, or the onboard Crew Medical Officer when Earth is far away. A timed, gamified daily routine and a personal logbook catch slow changes against each astronaut's own baseline. Real NASA data is built in: ISS cabin and radiation data, Inspiration4 bloodwork, and NOAA space weather.

This matters because on the way to Mars, help is up to 24 minutes away, so astronauts must assess their own health and act. NeuroShield was tested on 36 mission scenarios and on open human datasets.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS
NeuroShield is a camera-free, explainable health self-assessment tool for astronauts. It runs as a web app in any browser, offline, with no installation, and it covers three missions: the ISS (microgravity, 0.5 s signal delay), a lunar base (0.17 g, 1.3 s) and a Mars base (0.38 g, up to 24 min). It works in four steps: measure, understand, act, and escalate when needed.

- Measure: 26 live signals and 28 daily indicators, in their real units. They come from wearable brain and body sensors (EEG drowsiness and workload, fNIRS brain oxygen, heart rate and HRV, SpO2, skin conductance, head motion), the vital signs named in the challenge (blood pressure, heart rate, blood sugar in mg/dL, body temperature, sleep, mood), habitat and suit sensors (CO2, O2, cabin pressure, CO, radiation, temperature, humidity, noise, acceleration, suit pressure) and photos (skin, eye/OCT, wound, ultrasound).
- Understand: every indicator has normal and caution limits taken from NASA standards and the medical literature, and each limit links to its source. A health score from 0 to 100 is calculated per body system and overall. 21 explainable rules use persistence, hysteresis and root-cause suppression, so alerts come early without flooding the crew.
- Act: every alert says why it fired and gives numbered steps (for example: mask up, move to the storm shelter, take 15 g of fast sugar, stop the EVA and repressurise).
- Escalate: the alert also says who leads. On the ISS that is the flight surgeon; at Mars it is the onboard Crew Medical Officer, because the ground is minutes away.

The app has seven tabs:
- Live Monitor: signal cards, health score, a clickable body map, alerts and an event log.
- Daily Check-in: a timed routine with "How?" step-by-step help, reminders, XP, streaks and badges, a reaction-time test (PVT), and a daily log with photo upload.
- Crew Logbook: 60 days of personal history, an anomaly map, detected episodes and a side-by-side photo comparison.
- Bloodwork: real Inspiration4 blood tests.
- Space Weather: live NOAA proton flux.
- AI Assistant: an offline demo that answers from the crew member's own data.
- Guide: every indicator with its range, how it is measured and its linked source, plus the HRP risk table and the dataset table.

The demo contains 12 scenarios for each of the three missions, 36 runs in total. Examples are fatigue leading to microsleep, a slow cabin leak, a high-G entry, a CO2 scrubber failure, low blood sugar, fever, a solar particle event, an EVA decompression risk and a cabin thermal failure. Each run is lived by four crew members, who each have their own baselines and react in their own way. A fourth mission, "Lab", replays real human recordings from open datasets.

BENEFITS

- Self-assessment at a glance: every signal is colour-coded (green / amber / red) against limits with linked sources, and a 0-100 health score per body system shows where the problem is. Astronauts know their status and what to do without waiting for Earth.

- Warnings come minutes early: in the fatigue scenario, drowsiness is flagged 4.6 minutes before the first microsleep. In the cabin-leak scenario, the pressure alert comes 96 seconds before blood oxygen falls. This leaves time to act before symptoms appear.

- Clear guidance in an emergency: each alert gives numbered steps and says who leads. On the ISS that is the flight surgeon; at Mars, where an answer can take up to 48 minutes, it is the Crew Medical Officer.

- Slow changes are caught early: the personal logbook compares each day with the astronaut's own baseline, not a population average. It finds sleep debt, signs of optic-disc swelling (SANS), weight loss or a rise in blood pressure days before they become serious.

- Measurements stay on track: a timed daily routine with step-by-step help, reminders and rewards (XP, streaks, badges) makes the daily checks easy to keep up on long missions.

- Private and independent: data stays on the device, and the app works offline with no installation, so it keeps working even when the link to Earth is lost.

INTENDED IMPACT
On long missions to the Moon and Mars, the crew becomes its own first responder. NeuroShield aims to make every astronaut ready for the minutes before help arrives. On Earth the same approach can help pilots, miners, divers and health workers in remote places. The next steps are to connect the NeuroShield wearable (the WebSocket input is ready), test volunteers on a motion simulator, run a small medical language model (MedGemma) on board, and run usability tests with analog-mission crews.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES, HARDWARE AND SOFTWARE
- App: HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript with no dependencies. Canvas charts, an SVG body map, localStorage and IndexedDB for on-device data, and WebSocket input for the wearable.
- Data: Python 3. The synthetic dataset generator uses only the standard library. Real data is processed with wfdb, SciPy, pandas and xlrd, run with uv.
- Evaluation: Node.js scripts run the unchanged browser modules over every scenario and every logbook.
- Real data: NASA OSDR Environmental Data Application (ISS cabin CO2 and radiation), NASA OSDR OSD-569/575 (Inspiration4 bloodwork), NOAA SWPC GOES proton flux, NASA Human Research Program risk documents and NASA-STD-3001. Open human datasets: PhysioNet Non-EEG, PRCP, BIDMC, NSR and Sleep-EDF, an EEG driver drowsiness dataset, Tufts fNIRS2MW and a VR cybersickness dataset.
- Deliverables: playwright-core and sharp for screenshots and video frames, ffmpeg, the Kokoro-82M text-to-speech model for the narration, pptxgenjs for the slides, and docx for the IEEE-format paper.
- Hardware: no physical hardware was used in the demo. Sensor streams are simulated or replayed from real recordings.
- AI assistance: Claude (Anthropic) helped with code and writing; the team reviewed the results.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE
- Camera-free: it works behind visors and masks and in darkness, and it records no faces.
- Minutes early: brain, body and cabin signals change before visible signs appear.
- Delay-aware: the guidance and who leads change with the distance from Earth.
- Personal baseline: each astronaut is compared with their own normal.
- Real NASA data is part of the core. The logbook's cabin CO2 comes from 60 real ISS days, including a real CO2 excursion, and Bloodwork scores the Inspiration4 crew against their own preflight values.
- Clear interface: colour coding, a clickable body figure, and gamification that keeps the daily routine on track.

FACTORS THE TEAM CONSIDERED
- Which measurements can actually be done in space: only wearables, fingerstick, saliva and urine kits, a fundoscope or OCT, and handheld ultrasound.
- Avoiding false alarms, so alerts stay trustworthy.
- Communication delay and who leads in an emergency.
- Privacy, offline use and on-device storage.
- Honesty about the data. The live and logbook signals are synthetic, based on literature models; real data is clearly labelled; the sample health images are drawn by code; and the weak spots of the rules are reported.
- Validation. On 36 scenarios the rules with no alerts in nominal runs. The logbook detector found 18 of 18 injected events. Open human datasets were used to correct the limits.
- NeuroShield is a decision-support prototype, not a medical device. It does not replace flight surgeons.
